## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/02.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Perspectives
“It takes intelligent people to take full advantage of intelligent machines”
 –Wooldridge, 1993

● An emerging problem in technology assisted instruction is the
 inauthentic manner in which software/technology and instruction are
 combined.

● Difference between inauthentic use and authentic use of
 technology (cognitive tool)

● To begin a discussion about how technology can be authentically
 utilized, investigate subjects where technology already plays an
 essential role.

10/30/26 Department of Educational Research, 2
 Measurement, and Evaluation, Boston College</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/03.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Purpose – Goal of the study
● To authentically incorporate the use of technology in an applied
 statistics class.

● To dissect the manner in which technology/software has been
 effectively incorporated into a graduate level introductory statistics

● To discern insights into the effective incorporation of software use in
 the classroom where software is an essential component of the
 subject

● To help educators from any discipline interrogate their own
 (in)authentic use of technology.

10/30/26 Department of Educational Research, 3
 Measurement, and Evaluation, Boston College</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/04.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Frameworks for the
Implementation of Technology
● Definition of “authentic”: Following Hennessy &amp; Murphy (1999), an
 activity is authentic if it is:
 ● coherent and personally meaningful, and
 ● purposeful within a social framework – the ordinary practices of
 culture
● To make judgments about the purposeful use of technology
 requires knowledge about how technology is used in society at
 large.

● Technology use in society at large leads to an investigation of
 expert knowledge.

● This aligns well with a large number of learning theories.

10/30/26 Department of Educational Research, 4
 Measurement, and Evaluation, Boston College</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/05.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Background
“Experts think with machines, they don’t let machines think for them.”

● Many of the implementations of technology in the statistics classroom
 are lacking due to an inauthentic use of the tools.

● Primary challenge: the seamless integration of computer software
 use with the development of theory in the class

● Limitations of the lecture/lab class format

● An attempt to overcome the limitation

10/30/26 Department of Educational Research, 5
 Measurement, and Evaluation, Boston College</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/06.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Background
● An authentic use of software requires an operating computer in
 the classroom that is projected in such as way so that all students
 can view the process as it takes place---teaching versus
 presenting.

● The limitation of PowerPoint: Distance between “the pointer” and
 “the voice”.

● Our solution to this dilemma: instead of projecting the software
 onto a basic reflective surface, the GUI is projected onto a touch
 sensitive white board (TSWB).

● Advantages of TSWB.

10/30/26 Department of Educational Research, 6
 Measurement, and Evaluation, Boston College</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/07.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Setting and Methodology
● Critical reflection of practice through participant observation

● The setting for the participant observations occurred at two
 different universities:
 ● In 5 classes where a TSWB was made available and
 ● in 6 classes without a TSWB
 ● Classes were no larger than 35 students

● How was TSWB used in class?

10/30/26 Department of Educational Research, 7
 Measurement, and Evaluation, Boston College</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/13.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Results
● A separate lab is no longer needed to demonstrate software use

● Richer and less contrived examples can be explored

● Students are exposed to an authentic discussion of theory and
 application

● A price for the teacher: mastery over 2 domains:
 ● subject matter and
 ● real-time use of the software

● Unexpected benefit for deaf students.

10/30/26 Department of Educational Research, 13
 Measurement, and Evaluation, Boston College</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/14.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Future of the Study
● The future of authentic instruction that incorporates technology/
 software lies with the interface between the technology/software
 and the subject matter which, in turn, is brought to life through the
 instructor’s fluency with that technology/software.

● In situations where technology/software has yet to find an
 essential niche within a discipline (or instructors are not fluent
 with its use) the result is usually inauthentic instruction relying
 upon highly contrived exercises.

● The key to authentic incorporation of technology in the classroom
 lies with the answer to the question: How do/would/should I, an
 expert, utilize technology in my own discipline specific research?

10/30/26 Department of Educational Research, 14
 Measurement, and Evaluation, Boston College</div>
```
